segments.voice: Yesterday we opened Shanti and Anushasana: Krishna stepped aside, and Bhishma, cleared of pain, began to teach. Did you get to ask an elder your question? Today, the first lesson. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

What is a king for? It sounds like a question for a political science class, but on the field it's urgent. Yudhishthira wears the crown now, and he still half wants to run. So he asks his grandfather, plainly, what the duties of a king are. Bhishma's answer fills a long section of the Shanti Parva, known as Rajadharma, the dharma of kings. It's practical, sometimes blunt, full of advice about treasuries, spies and alliances. But in the middle of it, there are a few pictures that stick. Today, two of them: a pond full of fish, and a mother carrying a child.
screen: `WHAT IS A KING FOR?` → `RAJADHARMA.` → `FISH, AND A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the fish. Bhishma describes what happens when there's no one to keep order. The strong devour the weak, he says, the way big fish eat the little ones in the water. Without protection, nobody's property is safe, nobody's family is safe, and the strong do whatever they like. The point isn't that kings are grand. It's that the weak need someone standing between them and the strong. In Bhishma's teaching, that's the job. Protection comes before glory. Second, the mother. Bhishma says a king should act like an expectant mother. A woman carrying a child, in his picture, sets aside some of the things she'd like for herself, for the good of the child she's carrying. So a king sets aside his own likes for the good of his people. That's a striking image for a warrior to use, from a man who took a vow never to marry or have children. The ruler, in his teaching, isn't the one being served. He's the one carrying. Then there's the warning running underneath. Bhishma tells Yudhishthira again and again to be gentle without being weak, and firm without being cruel. A king who is always soft gets ignored, and one who is always harsh gets feared and hated. So that's Rajadharma, in two pictures. Stand between the big fish and the small ones. Carry your people the way a mother carries a child. And Yudhishthira, who wanted to run to the forest, is being told that ruling well is itself a kind of self-denial. Peace, for him, may not mean escaping the throne. It may mean carrying it.
screen: `BIG FISH EAT THE SMALL` · `PROTECTION BEFORE GLORY` · `A KING LIKE AN EXPECTANT MOTHER` · then, large: `GENTLE, BUT NOT WEAK`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Shanti and Anushasana, Bhishma said a king stands between the big fish and the small, and carries his people like a mother. Did you stand up for someone smaller? Today, when the rules run out. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

Yudhishthira asks a hard question. What happens to dharma when everything falls apart? When there's war, famine, collapse, and the normal rules can't be kept? Bhishma's answer is a whole section called Apaddharma, dharma in times of distress. And to explain it, he tells a story that's uncomfortable on purpose. A great sage, Vishvamitra, is starving. The rains have failed for a long time. The fields are dust, the villages empty, and people are eating whatever they can find. One night, half dead, Vishvamitra slips into a poor hamlet looking for food. Today, what he finds, and who stops him.
screen: `WHEN THE RULES RUN OUT.` → `APADDHARMA.` → `A STARVING SAGE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In one hut, Vishvamitra sees a piece of dog meat hanging, the haunch of a dog. For a man of his station, by the rules of his world, this is deeply forbidden food. He decides to steal it anyway. But the man who lives there wakes up and catches him. And what follows isn't a fight. It's a debate. The householder, a man the society of that time placed at the bottom, argues for the rules. You're a sage, he says. You know dharma. Don't do this. Even I wouldn't advise it. Vishvamitra argues back. Staying alive comes first, he says, because only the living can practice dharma at all. When I'm through this, I'll make amends with austerity. A dead sage helps no one. The householder isn't fully convinced, but Vishvamitra takes the meat. Even now, the story says, he means to offer it to the gods before he eats. And then the god Indra sends rain, and the plants and the people revive. The story leaves the discomfort in place. The great sage steals. The man at the bottom lectures him on dharma. And Bhishma's point, telling it to the new king, is that dharma in a disaster isn't the same as dharma on an ordinary day. Rules exist to protect life. When keeping them would end life, a wise person may have to bend them, and then repair what they broke. But Bhishma also warns that this is for real distress, not for convenience. A king who calls every inconvenience a famine, in effect, has missed the lesson.
screen: `THE FORBIDDEN FOOD` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER ARGUES FOR THE RULES` · `"ONLY THE LIVING PRACTICE DHARMA"` · then, large: `FOR REAL DISTRESS ONLY`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind a time you bent one of your own rules because things were falling apart. Breathe in, and remember what was at stake. Breathe out, and ask honestly: was it real distress, or just convenience? Don't judge yourself, just look. If something wasn't repaired afterward, notice that too. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shanti and Anushasana. Today, Apaddharma: dharma for times of distress, told through a starving sage and the man who argued with him.

screen: `SHANTI AND ANUSHASANA.` · `WHEN THE RULES RUN OUT.`

segments.voice: A storm breaks over the forest. A hunter, a hard man who lives by trapping birds, is caught out in it, soaked and shaking with cold. In his cage is a female pigeon he caught that day. He stumbles to a big tree and crouches under it for shelter. He doesn't know that the tree is her home. Up in its branches her mate is grieving, wondering where she's gone. And from inside the cage, she can hear him. Yudhishthira had asked Bhishma about a person who gives shelter to someone who comes asking for it. This is the story Bhishma tells. Today, the pigeons and the hunter.
screen: `A STORM IN THE FOREST.` → `A HUNTER UNDER THEIR TREE.` → `SHE HEARS HER MATE.`

segments.voice: The female pigeon calls up to her mate, and what she says is startling. Don't grieve for me, she tells him. This man has come to our home, cold and hungry. He's our guest. Treat him as one. And the male pigeon does. He fetches a burning ember from somewhere and gathers dry leaves, and he makes a fire so the hunter can warm himself. Then he realizes he has nothing to feed his guest. He has no store of grain, nothing set aside. So he does the only thing he can think of. He offers himself, and drops into the fire, so the hunter will have food. The hunter is undone. The man who caught birds for a living has just watched a bird give its life to feed him. He opens the cage and lets the female go. But she, grieving her mate, follows him into the fire too. And the story says the two of them rise to heaven together, shining. The hunter can't go back to who he was. He throws away his nets and his cage, gives up hunting, and goes off into the forest to live in austerity. The word underneath all of this is atithi, the guest. In the dharma Bhishma teaches, a guest who comes to your door is to be honored, whoever they are, even an enemy, even the person who hurt you. It's an extreme story, and the text tells it as extreme. Bhishma isn't asking the new king to leap into fires. He's showing him how far hospitality reaches: past fairness, past safety, all the way to the person who did you harm.

865.howItsDone: The story of Gautami, the snake, Death and Time is retold by Hindu teachers when they speak of karma and of letting go of revenge, and it stands at the opening of the Anushasana Parva.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Shanti and Anushasana, a pigeon honored the hunter who trapped his mate, and the hunter laid down his nets. Did you give someone an unexpected welcome? Today, the Anushasana opens. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

After all of Bhishma's teaching, Yudhishthira is still stuck in the same place. I caused all this, he says. I'm the reason you're lying on those arrows. So when the Anushasana Parva opens, Bhishma answers him with a story about blame. An old woman named Gautami finds her son dead. A snake has bitten him. A hunter, Arjunaka, catches the snake, ties it with a cord, and drags it to her. Tell me how to kill it, he says. Fire, or cut it to pieces? Either is fine with me. Today, what Gautami answers.
screen: `"I CAUSED ALL THIS."` → `A BOY BITTEN BY A SNAKE.` → `"HOW SHALL I KILL IT?"`

segments.voice: Gautami says: let it go. Killing it won't bring my son back, and it won't make me any less sad. The hunter argues; surely the guilty should pay. And then the snake speaks up. Don't blame me, it says. I didn't act on my own. Death sent me. And Death, Mrityu, appears. Don't blame me either, says Death. I was directed by Time. Then Time itself, Kala, arrives. And Time says: none of us is the real cause. The boy's own past actions brought him here, his karma. We were only the instruments. Gautami listens, and accepts it. The hunter lets the snake go. Death and Time depart. That's a strange chain, and Bhishma means it to be. Each one in the line points at the next, and the chain ends not in a villain but in the long working of actions and their results. Now look at who Bhishma is telling it to. Yudhishthira is sure he's the snake. He believes the deaths are on him alone. Bhishma is saying, gently, that you are one link in something much longer, and you are not the whole of it. This isn't permission to stop caring. It's a way out of the kind of guilt that eats a person alive and helps nobody. And notice who sees it first. Not the warrior, not the king. A grieving old mother, the one with every reason to want revenge, is the one who says let it go. Anushasana means instruction, and its opening lesson, in this story, is about where blame stops.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Shanti and Anushasana, Gautami told the hunter to let the snake go, and the chain of blame ran back through Death and Time. Did you find one more link? Today, the teacher's last lesson. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

Bhishma carries an unusual gift. Long ago, his father blessed him so that death would come to him only when he chose it. So he has been lying on the arrows, teaching, and waiting. He's waiting for a particular turning of the year: the time when the sun begins its northward course, called uttarayana, which the tradition holds as an auspicious time to die. Bhishma sent Yudhishthira back to the city to rule. Now the season has turned, and Yudhishthira comes back to the field, with fire and garlands and everything needed for the last rites. Today, how Bhishma goes.
screen: `DEATH ONLY WHEN HE CHOOSES.` → `WAITING FOR THE SUN TO TURN.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Bhishma opens his eyes and sees them all around him: Yudhishthira and his brothers, Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Krishna. He says the time has come. He speaks a few last words to Dhritarashtra, the blind king, whose sons are gone, and tells him not to grieve, and to treat the Pandavas as his own. Then he turns to Krishna and asks for leave to go. Notice that. A man who can choose his own death still asks permission to take it. Krishna gives it. And then Bhishma does something the text describes almost like a meditation. He draws his life breath inward, part by part. As it withdraws from each limb, the story says, the arrows in that part of his body fall away and the wound closes. Limb by limb, the bed of arrows lets him go. At last the breath leaves through the crown of his head, rising like a great light into the sky. His family builds the pyre and performs the rites. Then they go down to the Ganga to offer water, and the river goddess herself rises out of it, weeping. Bhishma was her son. She grieves that he fell to Shikhandi. And Krishna comforts her: it was Arjuna who brought him down, he says, with Shikhandi only standing in front, and her son has gone to the heavens. Don't grieve. So the teaching from the bed of arrows ends without a speech: a man finishing his work, asking leave, and going when it's time, while the arrows fall from him one by one.

867.title: Ashvamedhika
867.hook: the war is won, the funeral rites are done, and the new king falls down on the riverbank and can't get up
867.howItsDone: The Ashvamedhika Parva is the book of the Mahabharata that follows Bhishma's teachings; Hindus hear it in recitations of the full epic, and the horse sacrifice is remembered as a great royal rite of the Vedic world.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the long sessions of Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma teaching from his bed of arrows, and then letting go. What stayed with you from all that advice? Today a new book opens. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

The water offerings for Bhishma have been poured into the Ganga. The great teacher is gone. Yudhishthira has listened to him at length, about kingship, about duty, about peace. He has the crown. He has the kingdom. And at the riverbank, in Ganguli's telling, he simply goes down, collapses on the bank, overwhelmed by grief. Bhima holds him. Krishna speaks to him. The old blind king Dhritarashtra, whose own sons died in this war, is the one who tells him to get up. A new book of the epic opens with a king on the ground. Its name is today's word.
screen: `THE OFFERINGS ARE POURED.` → `THE KING FALLS ON THE BANK.` → `THE BLIND KING SAYS: GET UP.`

segments.voice: Ashvamedhika is the book of the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice: a great royal rite in which a consecrated horse is let loose to wander, guarded by warriors, and the kingdoms it passes through either welcome it or fight. Yudhishthira doesn't come up with the idea. He wants to leave the throne and go to the forest. It's the sage Vyasa who tells him that grief is not a plan. Perform sacrifices, Vyasa says, give gifts, take up the work of a king; the horse sacrifice will cleanse what weighs on you. And Yudhishthira's answer is very practical. There's no money. The war has emptied the treasury. The kings who might have sent tribute are dead, and he will not squeeze grieving people for more. So Vyasa tells him an old story. Long ago, a king named Marutta held a sacrifice in the Himalayas so lavish that the gold left behind was too much to carry away. It's still there in the mountains, Vyasa says. Go and bring it. See what the epic is doing here. The victors don't get a parade. They get a man who can't stand up, a dead treasury, and a sage pointing at an old king's leftover gold. The way forward runs through someone else's generosity, long ago. Over the next days, this book will bring a forgotten teaching, an angry sage, a child who comes back to life, a son who fights his father, and a strange little animal with half a golden body. It begins with getting up.

868.title: Ashvamedhika
868.hook: after the war, in a quiet palace hall, Arjuna admits to Krishna that he has forgotten the teaching he heard on the battlefield
868.howItsDone: The Anugita is read by students of the Mahabharata alongside the Bhagavad Gita, and commentators and teachers in several Hindu traditions have discussed how the two teachings relate.

segments.voice: Yesterday Ashvamedhika opened with Yudhishthira on the riverbank, an empty treasury, and Vyasa pointing to old King Marutta's gold. Who offered you something practical lately? Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

I've forgotten it. That, in plain terms, is what Arjuna tells Krishna. The war is over. The two friends are walking together in the great assembly hall the Pandavas have won back, with time on their hands at last. And Arjuna brings up the conversation in the chariot, between the two armies, before the fighting began. The teaching people now call the Bhagavad Gita. What you told me then, he says, has slipped away from my mind. Please tell it to me again. Today, Krishna's answer.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `A WALK IN THE HALL.` → `"I'VE FORGOTTEN IT."`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't pretend that's fine. In Ganguli's telling, he's displeased. You didn't hold on to what I told you in confidence, he says, and I'm sorry you forgot it. And then he says something surprising: he can't simply repeat it. What he spoke on the battlefield, he explains, he spoke while united in yoga, and he can't call it back word for word. So instead he tells Arjuna an old story. A brahmana meets a perfected sage, a siddha, and asks him the big questions: how a living being dies, how it is born again, what binds it to action, and how it goes free. The siddha answers at length. Then come more old dialogues: a brahmana and his wife, a teacher and his student. Together these chapters are known as the Anugita. They return to the Gita's ground, the self, action and freedom, but in a different shape: no army, no chariot, no crisis. Just questions asked in peace. There's something honest about this. That first conversation happened between two armies, with the war about to begin, and afterward even Arjuna, who heard it face to face, lost hold of it. Insight doesn't keep by itself. The teacher's answer isn't a recording. It's a new conversation, built for a calmer day. Krishna doesn't hand Arjuna the old words. He sits down in the hall and starts again.
screen: `KRISHNA IS DISPLEASED` · `"I SPOKE IT IN YOGA"` · `A SAGE ANSWERS A BRAHMANA` · then, large: `THE ANUGITA: THE TEACHING RETOLD`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring back one thing you once understood clearly, a lesson, a promise to yourself, something someone wise told you, that has faded since. Don't try to recover all of it. Breathe in and find just one sentence of it. Breathe out and say it to yourself quietly, in your own words, as if for the first time. If you pray, you can ask in your own way to keep hold of it. The bell holds the time.
Ashvamedhika. The book where Arjuna admits he has forgotten, and Krishna teaches again, in a new shape.
Your line: Ashvamedhika. Today, ask someone to remind you of something you've lost hold of, and don't be embarrassed to ask. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.
